01.event: sent a question to Rabbi Helbo
01.missing: Any event beyond sending a question; the passage is a fragment of a question.
01.reason: Sending a question is a quasi-speech-act with no conflict and no further event; it is the frame of a halakhic question and answer.

02.event: He habitually bent down so his mother could climb into and out of bed on him, then came and praised himself in the study hall.
02.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half the honor due, citing a mother throwing a purse into the sea.
02.outcome: His boast is deflated; he is shown the measure he has not reached.
02.summary: Rabbi Tarfon honored his mother by letting her step on him to get into and out of bed. He came and boasted of this in the study hall. The Sages answered that he had not reached even half of the honor due to her.
02.reason: A habitual frame followed by a one-time event (his boasting in the study hall) and a response that reverses his self-assessment; actions plus a change, not just a custom.

03.actor: a man, his daughter, the orphan heirs
03.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter; the heirs divided the estate and gave her none.
03.turn: Rav Yosef thought it matched the mishna; Abaye distinguished it.
03.outcome: Abaye prescribes that they give her a tree and redivide; no outcome is narrated.
03.summary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter in his will, but the orphans divided the property without giving her one. Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna; Abaye rejected the comparison and said they must give her a tree and divide afresh.
03.missing: Whether anything happened after the ruling.
03.reason: There is an incident with more than one action (the bequest, the heirs' division withholding the tree) followed by legal discussion and a prescribed remedy; like the cow case it has a narrated wrong, but the passage is mostly discussion with no narrated outcome.

04.event: They disagreed for two and a half years about whether man should have been created.
04.outcome: They concluded it would have been better not to be created, but now one should examine one's deeds.
04.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued for two and a half years over whether it would be better for man not to have been created. They were counted and concluded that it would have been better not to be, but that now one must scrutinize his deeds.
04.missing: Any event beyond the debate and the vote.
04.reason: Mainly a scholarly disagreement (speech), but a prolonged dispute ending in a vote is a minimal event with a resolution; between borderline and not, borderline is preferred.

05.event: A ritual bath in Yavne presumed complete was measured and found deficient; the two disputed the status of past immersions.
05.turn: Through an exchange of parables Rabbi Akiva's analysis prevails.
05.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon concedes and praises Akiva: whoever separates from you separates from life.
05.summary: A mikveh in Yavne thought to be full was measured and found deficient. Rabbi Tarfon ruled the past immersions pure and Rabbi Akiva impure, and they argued by parables. Akiva's reasoning won, and Tarfon conceded with high praise for him.
05.reason: There is a real incident (the measured mikveh) and a change (Tarfon's concession), but after the incident it is all legal argument; R-C7 shape 1, mainly speech with an event.

06.event: He went as agent to betroth a woman for his son.
06.turn: Her family refused to give her to the son.
06.outcome: He betrothed her to himself, fearing someone else would take her meanwhile.
06.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman on behalf of his son but ended up betrothing her to himself. The Gemara explains that her family would not give her to the son, and that he feared someone else would betroth her if he delayed.
06.missing: The explanatory details are the Gemara's answers to a difficulty, not narrated events.
06.reason: A real incident with a turn (going for the son, marrying her himself), but it is a short report cited and then explained by the Gemara's own resolution of a difficulty; events with little development, so borderline rather than a full story.

07.event: Ravina examined a slaughterer's knife in Babylonia during his teacher's lifetime.
07.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him; Ravina cited Rav Hamnuna's precedent.
07.outcome: Ravina argued he was a disciple-colleague; nothing further happens.
07.summary: Ravina examined a knife in Babylonia while his teacher Rav Ashi was alive. Rav Ashi asked why, and Ravina justified himself by the precedent of Rav Hamnuna, arguing he was a disciple-colleague.
07.missing: Any event or change after the exchange.
07.reason: Segments 2-3 are bare reports of practice; the Ravina exchange is one act followed by ordinary scholarly challenge and justification, with nothing changing afterwards.

08.missing: Any narrated event; this is Rav Kahana's exegetical explanation of how the virgins of Jabesh-gilead were identified.
08.reason: An exegetical elaboration of a biblical episode (Judges 21); at most a midrashic retelling of biblical events, which is out of scope, and it is presented as an answer to a question rather than a story.

09.actor: Rabbi Banai and the orphan daughters
09.event: The orphan daughters came before Shmuel regarding property held by Rabbi Banai.
09.outcome: Shmuel ordered him to sustain them.
09.summary: Rabbi Banai held movable property belonging to orphans. The daughters came before Shmuel, who told him to sustain them.
09.missing: Any narrated action or change besides coming to court and the ruling.
09.reason: This is the exact case Jeff ruled not a story: coming before a rabbi and being ruled on, with the outcome only implied.

10.missing: Any event; the passage is statements and reported practices about orla outside the Land.
10.reason: Levi's request and the rabbis' practice of supplying each other are bare reports of practice cited as halakhic evidence, with nothing following.

11.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yohanan
11.event: A case like the earlier one came before Rabbi Yohanan; Reish Lakish raised his objection.
11.turn: Rabbi Yohanan answered exactly as Rabbi Elazar had earlier.
11.outcome: Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
11.summary: On another occasion a case about establishing priestly status came before Rabbi Yohanan. Reish Lakish asked his usual question and Rabbi Yohanan gave the very answer Rabbi Elazar had given before. Reish Lakish then glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not quoting Rabbi Yohanan.
11.reason: Mainly speech, but there is interpersonal conflict and a non-verbal act (the harsh look) with a realization; R-C7 shape 1 places it as borderline.

12.missing: Any one-time event; the passage reports a custom of drawing water cited as proof.
12.reason: A bare report of a practice (residents drew water on Shabbat with the Elders' approval) cited as evidence, with no event following.

13.event: Bar Shatya, sometimes insane, sold property.
13.turn: Two pairs of witnesses contradicted each other about his state at the sale.
13.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled the testimonies cancel and the land stays with Bar Shatya.
13.summary: Bar Shatya, who was intermittently insane, sold property. Two witnesses said he sold while sane and two said while insane. Rav Ashi ruled the testimonies cancel and the land remains in Bar Shatya's possession.
13.missing: Any narrated consequence; the case is cited as legal proof.
13.reason: An incident with more than one action (the sale, conflicting testimonies) followed by a ruling, close to the cow case; but it is cited inside the legal discussion with no narrated change, so it sits at borderline.

14.event: A man snatched coins from another and threw them to a woman washing her feet, declaring her betrothed.
14.outcome: Rava ruled the coins were stolen and the betrothal void.
14.summary: A woman was washing her feet when a man grabbed coins from someone else, threw them to her and declared her betrothed to him. The matter came before Rava, who ruled that since the owner had not despaired of the stolen coins, she was not betrothed.
14.reason: Exactly the R-C0 cow shape: a certain man committed narrated acts (snatched, threw, declared) and a rabbi ruled; the ruling resolves an incident with real actions.

15.actor: Rabbi Abbahu and his attendant Rabbi Nahum
15.event: Rabbi Abbahu walked leaning on his attendant, who gathered rulings from him.
15.outcome: A series of questions and answers about unattributed mishnayot.
15.summary: Rabbi Abbahu used to walk leaning on Rabbi Nahum, who would ask him halakhic questions along the way. The rest is a sequence of questions and answers on legal principle.
15.missing: Any event beyond the setting and the questions and answers.
15.reason: A setting followed by questions and answers is not a story (Shabbat 147a ruling); teaching speech with no conflict or change.

16.event: A woman whose husband was overseas gave birth twelve months after he left.
16.outcome: Rava Tosfa'a declared the child legitimate.
16.summary: A woman's husband went overseas and she gave birth twelve months later. Rava Tosfa'a ruled the child fit. The Gemara cites this to ask whose opinion he followed.
16.missing: Narration of the incident itself; it is cited as a precedent within the discussion.
16.reason: One circumstance followed by a ruling, cited as evidence in a legal argument, with nothing else narrated; under R-C0's 2026-10-25 limit this is not a story.

17.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza.
17.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the challenge, relying on Rav Zevid of Nehardea.
17.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza. Rav Ashi questioned the basis, but Ameimar held to his ruling because he had heard it from Rav Zevid.
17.missing: Any action beyond a ruling and a scholarly challenge.
17.reason: A ruling followed by ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, with no change; not conflict in the R-C2 sense.

18.missing: Any event beyond Rabbi Tavla seeing a bolt and not objecting, cited as a proof and rebutted.
18.reason: A bare report cited as evidence within the legal discussion (Rabbi Tavla saw and said nothing); nothing follows.

19.actor: Rav Pappa, Yehuda bar Mareimar, Abba of Sura
19.event: Rav Pappa went to write his son's marriage contract; Yehuda bar Mareimar escorted him but would not enter.
19.turn: Rav Pappa forced him to enter; he sat silent, and Abba of Sura, thinking him angry, signed over everything he owned as dowry.
19.outcome: Yehuda said he did not want it; Abba offered to retract, and Yehuda told him not to make himself one who retracts.
19.summary: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's bride, the daughter of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to escort him but refused to enter, not wanting to pressure the father. Rav Pappa forced him in; he sat silently, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, wrote all his property into the dowry. Yehuda said he had not wanted that, and when Abba offered to retract, told him he should not become a man who retracts.
19.reason: Multiple actions (escorting, forcing entry, silence, writing over the estate), misunderstanding, causality and change; a full narrative.

20.event: An incident of this kind occurred.
20.turn: Rafram pressured Rav Ashi to rule.
20.outcome: Rav Ashi collected the full value of the document.
20.summary: There was a case of this kind; Rafram pressed Rav Ashi, who ruled that the full value of the note be collected.
20.missing: The incident itself is not narrated, only named.
20.reason: An unnarrated case plus a ruling, where the pressure is speech; nothing but a ruling is told, so under R-C0's limit it is not a story.
